title: The Simulator — How Security Proofs Work

questions.question: What does it mean for a protocol to be zero-knowledge?
options: A simulator can produce the verifier's view without the witness, so the verifier learns nothing beyond the statement being true
The proof transcript is encrypted so the verifier cannot read it
The prover never sends any information to the verifier
The prover's secret is hidden inside a hash function
questions.explanation: Zero-knowledge: for every verifier V*, there exists a PPT simulator S(x) (no witness) whose output is computationally indistinguishable from the real view. The simulation's existence proves the view contains no information about the witness.

questions.question: In a Schnorr sigma protocol, why does the simulator pick c and s before computing R?
options: To back-compute R = g^s · pk^{-c}, making the transcript satisfy g^s == R · pk^c without knowing the secret
Because the challenge c must be sent before the commitment R in the protocol
To avoid computing discrete logarithms
Because the response s must be chosen before the verifier sees the commitment
questions.explanation: The honest prover commits R = g^r first, then receives c, then computes s = r+cx. The simulator reverses this: pick c, s freely, then set R = g^s · pk^{-c}. The verification equation holds by construction, without needing x.

questions.question: A sigma protocol has special soundness. What does this mean?
options: Given two valid transcripts (R, c1, s1) and (R, c2, s2) with c1≠c2, one can extract the witness x
The protocol is secure against quantum adversaries
The challenge c must be special (non-interactive) to be secure
The prover only needs to send one message instead of three
questions.explanation: Special soundness: two accepting transcripts with the same commitment R but different challenges c1≠c2 allow computing x = (s1-s2)·(c1-c2)^{-1} mod order. This knowledge extractor proves the prover 'knows' the witness.

questions.question: In the Schnorr protocol, why are real and simulated transcripts identically distributed?
options: In both cases, (c, s) are uniformly random; R is then determined by the verification equation and (c, s, pk)
The simulator uses the same random tape as the prover
The commitment R is always set to g^1 = g in both cases
Real and simulated transcripts have different distributions — the simulation is only computationally indistinguishable
questions.explanation: Real: c uniform, s = r+cx uniform (since r is fresh uniform). Sim: c, s both explicitly uniform. In both cases (c, s) are i.i.d. uniform, and R is then uniquely determined by g^s = R·pk^c. So the joint distribution of (R, c, s) is identical — this is perfect ZK.

questions.question: Why does parallel composition break zero-knowledge for the basic Schnorr protocol?
options: If the prover reuses the same r for two rounds, an adversary seeing (s1, s2) with different challenges (c1, c2) can compute x = (s1-s2)/(c1-c2)
Parallel composition always breaks ZK because two messages are sent simultaneously
The simulator cannot handle two verifiers at once
The group order is too small for two simultaneous protocols
questions.explanation: With shared r: s1 = r+c1·x, s2 = r+c2·x, so s1-s2 = (c1-c2)·x, revealing x. The simulator also fails: it cannot program two independent challenges for the same commitment simultaneously (that would require solving discrete log).

questions.question: What is the Fiat-Shamir transform and how does the simulator handle it?
options: Replace the interactive challenge c with H(R || pk || m) in a ROM; the simulator programs H(R_sim || pk || m) = c_sim before committing to R_sim
Replace the commitment R with a hash of the witness
Apply the simulator in the standard model without a random oracle
Hash both the commitment and response together to bind them
questions.explanation: Fiat-Shamir: c = H(R || pk || m). The simulator (in ROM) picks c and s first, back-computes R = g^s·pk^{-c}, then programs H(R || pk || m) = c. Since the adversary hasn't queried this input yet, the programming is undetectable.

questions.question: What is the difference between HVZK (honest-verifier zero-knowledge) and full ZK?
options: HVZK: simulator only works when the verifier sends a uniform random challenge. Full ZK: simulator works for any (malicious) verifier that may bias the challenge
HVZK: the prover is honest. Full ZK: the verifier is honest
HVZK: requires a random oracle. Full ZK: works in the standard model
HVZK and full ZK are identical for sigma protocols
questions.explanation: HVZK: verifier follows the protocol exactly (sends uniform c). The Schnorr simulator works here. Full ZK: for ANY verifier strategy, including biased or adaptive challenges. Achieving full ZK from sigma protocols usually requires additional techniques (e.g., commitments to the challenge).

questions.question: In a simulation-based security proof, what role does the simulator play?
options: It constructs the adversary's view in the ideal world, proving that the real and ideal worlds are indistinguishable
It runs the real protocol on behalf of the prover
It extracts the witness from a cheating prover
It generates the trusted setup parameters
questions.explanation: The simulator S(x) produces the ideal-world view without the witness w. If Real_view ≈_c Ideal_view = S(x), then no information about w leaks from the protocol — because whatever the adversary/verifier sees could have been generated by S alone.
